title: Information Retrieval: Information Embedding
text:
Stéphane Marchand-Maillet Department of Computer Science Master in Computer Science – Spring Semester



Documents present themselves as a list of words (terms). It is necessary to define a vocabulary, i.e., the set of relevant terms, and then to represent these terms or the documents in a form (features) that the computer can manipulate: vector, distribution, etc.
This representation, called an embedding, is the cornerstone of any information retrieval system.




We use the following notation:

A collection of \(N\) documents (raw texts) is given.
\(\mathbf{d}_j\) is the representation of the \(j\)-th document. The space (and its dimension) containing \(\mathbf{d}_j\) depends on the chosen representation.
We define a vocabulary of \(M\) terms, whose representation is \(\mathbf{t}_i\).
\(\mathbf{I}_j \subseteq [M]\) is the list of indices of terms contained in document \(j\).





The Boolean model is the simplest: it encodes the vocabulary and the collection via one-hot encoding (binary embedding).

The \(i\)-th term is represented by a vector of dimension \(M\): \[ \mathbf{t}_i = [\delta_{ik}]_{k=1}^{M} \] where \(\delta_{ik}\) equals \(1\) if \(i=k\), \(0\) otherwise.
The \(j\)-th document is represented by the conjunction (Boolean sum) of the vectors of all the terms it contains: \[ \mathbf{d}_j = \bigvee_{i \in \mathbf{I}_j} \mathbf{t}_i \] Documents and terms are therefore located at the vertices of the hypercube \([0,1]^M\).
A query \(q\) is expressed as a logical expression (with AND, OR, NOT operators) and translated into conjunctive components, which are compared to each document.

The return value (Retrieval Status Value, RSV) is binary: \[ \mathrm{RSV}(\mathbf{d}_j, q) \in \{0,1\} \]


Query: \(q =\) (Geneva \(\land\) particle) \(\lor\) CERN

Document “Particle physics is well-studied in Geneva” → relevant.
Document “CERN leads the search for W boson” → relevant.
Document “EU invests in searching for new particles” → not relevant.
Document “Geneva is a place for scientific research” → not relevant.
Document “The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog” → not relevant.

This “all or nothing” character lacks flexibility: we desire a continuous value in \([0,1]\).





Terms are considered independent and unordered. Their multiplicity is taken into account: we speak of a bag rather than a set. Structure (paragraphs, title, etc.) is lost.


The basic hypothesis: the more a word appears in a document, the more it represents it.
\[ f_{ij} = \text{number of occurrences of term } i \text{ in document } j \]



We wish to account for the discriminative power of a term within the collection.
\[ \mathrm{idf}_i \stackrel{\text{def}}{=} \log\left(\frac{n_i}{N}\right)^{-1} = \log\frac{N}{n_i} \] where \(n_i\) is the number of documents containing term \(i\).
A term present in all documents (\(n_i \approx N\)) is not discriminative (\(\mathrm{idf}_i \approx 0\)).



The weight of term \(i\) in document \(j\) is defined by: \[ w_{ij} = tf_{ij} \cdot idf_i \]
The term-document matrix \(\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}\) contains these weights. This is the TF-IDF embedding.

Document \(j\) is represented by the column vector (or row vector, depending on convention): \[ \mathbf{d}_j = [w_{1j}, w_{2j}, \dots, w_{Mj}]^\top \]
Term \(i\) is represented by its presence across the collection: \[ \mathbf{t}_i = [w_{i1}, w_{i2}, \dots, w_{iN}]^\top \]




We can write: \[ \mathbf{d}_j = \sum_{i=1}^M w_{ij} \mathbf{e}_i = \sum_{i=1}^M tf_{ij}\, (idf_i\, \mathbf{e}_i) = \sum_{i=1}^M tf_{ij}\, \boldsymbol{\tau}_i \] where \(\boldsymbol{\tau}_i = idf_i\, \mathbf{e}_i\) is the discriminative basis.
Thus, \(idf_i\) (common to all documents) scales dimension \(i\), and \(tf_{ij}\) is the real coordinate of the document in this basis.





Embeddings are the basis of many retrieval models. In the vector model, a geometric similarity, generally cosine, is used between document and query vectors.



Documents are vectors \(\mathbf{d}_j \in \mathbb{R}^M\) (obtained via TF-IDF).
A query is considered as a document example (Query by Example, QbE) and is projected into the same space: \(\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^M\).
Relevance is evaluated by a similarity between \(\mathbf{d}_j\) and \(\mathbf{q}\).




A naive idea would be to use the Euclidean distance \(\|\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{d}_j\|\), but the bag-of-words structure suggests instead a set intersection measure.
In the set-based version, if \(\hat{\mathbf{d}}_j\) is the set of terms in the document and \(\hat{\mathbf{q}}\) is that of the query, then \[ \mathrm{RSV}(\hat{\mathbf{d}}_j, \hat{\mathbf{q}}) = |\hat{\mathbf{d}}_j \cap \hat{\mathbf{q}}| \]
In the binary vector space, this corresponds to the dot product: \[ \mathrm{RSV}(\mathbf{d}_j, \mathbf{q}) = \sum_i w_{ij} w_{iq} = \mathbf{d}_j^\top \mathbf{q} = \langle \mathbf{d}_j, \mathbf{q} \rangle \]



This idea is extended to different similarity measures, summarized in the table below.








Measure
Continuous Formula (real weights)
Binary Formula (0/1 weights)




Matching
\(\langle \mathbf{d}_j, \mathbf{q} \rangle\)
\(|\hat{\mathbf{d}}_j \cap \hat{\mathbf{q}}|\)


Cosine
\(\displaystyle \frac{\langle \mathbf{d}_j, \mathbf{q} \rangle}{\|\mathbf{d}_j\| \|\mathbf{q}\|}\)
\(\displaystyle \frac{|\hat{\mathbf{d}}_j \cap \hat{\mathbf{q}}|}{\sqrt{|\hat{\mathbf{d}}_j|}\sqrt{|\hat{\mathbf{q}}|}}\)


Dice
\(\displaystyle \frac{2\langle \mathbf{d}_j, \mathbf{q} \rangle}{\sum_i (w_{ij}+w_{iq})}\)
\(\displaystyle \frac{2|\hat{\mathbf{d}}_j \cap \hat{\mathbf{q}}|}{|\hat{\mathbf{d}}_j|+|\hat{\mathbf{q}}|}\)


Overlap
\(\displaystyle \frac{\langle \mathbf{d}_j, \mathbf{q} \rangle}{\min(\sum_i w_{ij},\sum_i w_{iq})}\)
\(\displaystyle \frac{|\hat{\mathbf{d}}_j \cap \hat{\mathbf{q}}|}{\min(|\hat{\mathbf{d}}_j|,|\hat{\mathbf{q}}|)}\)


Jaccard
\(\displaystyle \approx \frac{\langle \mathbf{d}_j, \mathbf{q} \rangle}{\sum_i \max(w_{ij},w_{iq})}\)
\(\displaystyle \frac{|\hat{\mathbf{d}}_j \cap \hat{\mathbf{q}}|}{|\hat{\mathbf{d}}_j \cup \hat{\mathbf{q}}|}\)



The most used measure is cosine similarity: \[ \mathrm{RSV}(\mathbf{d}_j, \mathbf{q}) = \cos\bigl(\angle(\mathbf{d}_j,\mathbf{q})\bigr) = \frac{\mathbf{d}_j^\top \mathbf{q}}{\|\mathbf{d}_j\| \|\mathbf{q}\|} = \frac{\sum_i w_{ij} w_{iq}}{\sqrt{\sum_i w_{ij}^2}\,\sqrt{\sum_i w_{iq}^2}} \]








If a retrieval system responds to each query by ranking documents in decreasing order of probability of usefulness to the user (these probabilities being estimated as accurately as possible from the available data), then the overall effectiveness of the system will be the best possible based on that data. — S.E. Robertson, 1977

We therefore seek to estimate \(\mathbb{P}(R \mid \mathbf{d}_j, q)\), where \(R\) is a binary random variable indicating relevance.



To avoid setting an absolute threshold, we use the odds ratio: \[ O(R \mid \mathbf{d}_j, q) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(R \mid \mathbf{d}_j, q)}{\mathbb{P}(\neg R \mid \mathbf{d}_j, q)} \]
By Bayes’ theorem: \[ O(R \mid \mathbf{d}_j, q) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{d}_j \mid R, q)}{\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{d}_j \mid \neg R, q)} \cdot \frac{\mathbb{P}(R \mid q)}{\mathbb{P}(\neg R \mid q)} \] Since \(\mathbb{P}(R \mid q)\) is constant for all documents, we have: \[ O(R \mid \mathbf{d}_j, q) \propto \frac{\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{d}_j \mid R, q)}{\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{d}_j \mid \neg R, q)} \]



If we assume that the log of the odds ratio is a linear function of the document’s features: \[ \log O(R \mid \mathbf{d}_j, q) = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{d}_j + w_0 \] then the probability of relevance is written: \[ \mathbb{P}(R \mid \mathbf{d}_j, q) = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{d}_j + w_0) \] with \(\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\) (logistic function).
The parameters \(\Theta = (\mathbf{w}, w_0)\) can be learned via gradient descent from examples of relevance (document, query, judgment).



We assume independence of term occurrences and their binary nature (presence/absence). For a document \(\mathbf{d}_j\), we denote by \(\mathcal{I}_j\) the set of present terms.
\[ \mathbb{P}(\mathbf{d}_j \mid R, q) = \prod_{i \in \mathcal{I}_j} \mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q) \prod_{i \notin \mathcal{I}_j} \bigl(1-\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q)\bigr) \]
Combining this with the expression for the odds ratio, we obtain: \[ O(R \mid \mathbf{d}_j, q) \propto \prod_{i \in \mathcal{I}_j} \frac{\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q)}{\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q)} \cdot \prod_{i \notin \mathcal{I}_j} \frac{1-\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q)}{1-\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q)} \]
After simplification (see course notes), we arrive at: \[ \log O(R \mid \mathbf{d}_j, q) \propto \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_j} \left[ \log \frac{\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q)}{1-\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q)} + \log \frac{1-\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q)}{\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q)} \right] \]
Only the query terms contribute, because for others \(\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q) = \mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q)\). We then define the return value: \[ \mathrm{RSV}(\mathbf{d}_j, q) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_j \cap \mathcal{I}_q} \left[ \log \frac{\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q)}{1-\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q)} + \log \frac{1-\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q)}{\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q)} \right] \]


We use pseudo-feedback: we take the top \(r\) returned documents as a training set \(S\).

\(r_i\): number of documents in \(S\) containing term \(i\).
\(n_i\): total number of documents containing term \(i\).

Initially (without feedback), we can take: \[ \mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q) = \text{constant} \quad\text{and}\quad \mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q) = \frac{n_i}{N} \] We then iterate with: \[ \mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q) = \frac{r_i}{r}, \qquad \mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q) = \frac{n_i - r_i}{N - r} \]




The BIR model was extended to give the BM25 (Okapi) formula, widely used.
The weight of a term \(i\) for a query \(q\) is: \[ w_i^{\text{RSJ}} = \log \frac{(r_i + 0.5)(N - R - n_i + r_i + 0.5)}{(n_i - r_i + 0.5)(R - r_i + 0.5)} \] where \(R\) is the number of known (or estimated) relevant documents.
The return value for a document \(j\) is then: \[ \mathrm{RSV}(\mathbf{d}_j, q) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_q} w_i^{\text{RSJ}} \cdot \frac{(k_1+1) tf_{ij}}{K + tf_{ij}} \cdot \frac{(k_3+1) tf_{iq}}{k_3 + tf_{iq}} \] with \[ K = k_1 \left( (1-b) + b \cdot \frac{dl_j}{avdl} \right) \]

\(dl_j\): length of document \(j\) (number of words),
\(avdl\): average document length,
\(k_1\), \(b\), \(k_3\): parameters (typically \(k_1=1.2\), \(b=0.75\), \(k_3=7\) or \(1000\)).








The TF-IDF embedding has weaknesses:

Synonymy: different terms (e.g., “car”, “automobile”) should have close representations.
Polysemy: the same term (e.g., “table”) can have multiple meanings; it should be broken down into multiple concepts.

We seek a basis of \(K\) concepts \(\{\mathbf{c}_k\}_{k=1}^K\), orthonormal (\(\langle \mathbf{c}_k, \mathbf{c}_l \rangle = \delta_{kl}\)), such that each term is a linear combination of these concepts: \[ \mathbf{t}_i = \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha_{ki} \mathbf{c}_k \]



The Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of a matrix \(\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}\) is written: \[ \mathbf{W} = \mathbf{U} \mathbf{\Sigma} \mathbf{V}^\top \] where \(\mathbf{U}\) and \(\mathbf{V}\) are orthogonal and \(\mathbf{\Sigma}\) is diagonal containing the singular values \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_{\min(M,N)}\).
Truncated SVD of rank \(K\) consists of keeping only the first \(K\) columns of \(\mathbf{U}\) and \(\mathbf{V}\) and the \(K\) largest singular values: \[ \mathbf{W}_K = \mathbf{U}_K \mathbf{\Sigma}_K \mathbf{V}_K^\top \]



We apply SVD to the term-document matrix \(\mathbf{W}\) (e.g., TF-IDF). We set: \[ \mathbf{W}_K = \mathbf{U}_K \mathbf{\Sigma}_K \mathbf{V}_K^\top \]
Then:

The columns of \(\mathbf{U}_K\) represent the \(K\) concepts (orthonormal vectors in the term space).
The rows of \(\mathbf{V}_K\) are the coordinates of the documents in this concept space.
The singular values indicate the importance of each concept.

We can project a document \(\mathbf{d}_j\) (TF-IDF vector) into the concept space by: \[ \tilde{\mathbf{d}}_j = \mathbf{\Sigma}_K^{-1} \mathbf{U}_K^\top \mathbf{d}_j \] Similarly for a query \(\mathbf{q}\): \[ \tilde{\mathbf{q}} = \mathbf{\Sigma}_K^{-1} \mathbf{U}_K^\top \mathbf{q} \]
Cosine similarity is then calculated in this reduced space: \[ \mathrm{RSV}(\mathbf{d}_j, \mathbf{q}) = \frac{\langle \tilde{\mathbf{d}}_j, \tilde{\mathbf{q}} \rangle}{\|\tilde{\mathbf{d}}_j\| \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}\|} \]



The concept space depends on the initial collection. To add new documents, two strategies exist:



Let \(\mathbf{D}\) be the TF-IDF representation of the new documents.
Project \(\mathbf{D}\) onto the existing space: \(\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{U}_K^\top \mathbf{D}\).
Calculate the residual \(\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{U}_K \mathbf{P}\).
Find an orthonormal basis \(\mathbf{B}\) for \(\mathbf{H}\) (via QR, SVD).
Project \(\mathbf{H}\) onto this basis: \(\mathbf{J} = \mathbf{B}^\top \mathbf{H}\).
Form \(\mathbf{Q} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{\Sigma}_K & \mathbf{P} \\ \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{J} \end{bmatrix}\) and compute its SVD: \(\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{U}_n \mathbf{\Sigma}_n \mathbf{V}_n^\top\).
The new SVD is obtained by: \[ [\,\mathbf{U}_K \ \mathbf{B}\,] \mathbf{U}_n \mathbf{\Sigma}_n \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{V}_K^\top & \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{I} \end{bmatrix} = [\,\mathbf{W}_K \ \mathbf{D}\,] \]





Simply project the new documents onto the existing space: \[ \hat{\mathbf{D}} = \mathbf{U}_K^\top \mathbf{D} \]
Concatenate the old and new projections: \[ [\,\mathbf{\Sigma}_K \mathbf{V}_K^\top \ \ \hat{\mathbf{D}}\,] \approx \mathbf{U}_K^\top [\,\mathbf{W}_K \ \mathbf{D}\,] \] This approximation is less expensive but less accurate.








Relevance to a query is central in information retrieval.
Documents are embedded into a feature space via embeddings.
The Boolean (binary) model lacks flexibility.
The Bag of Words (BoW) model relies on frequencies.
Cosine distance extends set intersection.
Probabilistic models estimate term relevance.
Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI) decorrelates TF-IDF dimensions by discovering latent factors (concepts) via SVD.
Non-linear equivalents exist, based on neural networks.






What is the Retrieval Status Value (RSV)?
Why is the Boolean model not flexible?
Define term frequency and inverse document frequency.
What is the link between these quantities and a tag cloud?
What information do these factors provide?
Describe the structure of a probabilistic retrieval model.
How can logistic regression be used in information retrieval?
Why is the Binary Independence Retrieval (BIR) model so named?
What is the odds ratio?
What is a concept in the LSI model?
In what sense does LSI decorrelate features?
Explain the fold-in strategy.





Information retrieval models are based on the notion of a term within a document. This applies to all types of media (text, image, audio…). The common objective is to estimate relevance. BoW, probabilistic, and LSI embeddings are constructed; neural embeddings are learned. All these models are classically implemented in software like Lucene.

\[ \mathbb{P}(\mathbf{d}_j \mid R, q) = \prod_{i \in \mathcal{I}_j} \mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q) \prod_{i \notin \mathcal{I}_j} \bigl(1-\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q)\bigr) \]
Combining this with the expression for the odds ratio, we obtain: \[ O(R \mid \mathbf{d}_j, q) \propto \prod_{i \in \mathcal{I}_j} \frac{\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q)}{\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q)} \cdot \prod_{i \notin \mathcal{I}_j} \frac{1-\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q)}{1-\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q)} \]
After simplification (see course notes), we arrive at: \[ \log O(R \mid \mathbf{d}_j, q) \propto \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_j} \left[ \log \frac{\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q)}{1-\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q)} + \log \frac{1-\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q)}{\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q)} \right] \]
Only the query terms contribute, because for others \(\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q) = \mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q)\). We then define the return value: \[ \mathrm{RSV}(\mathbf{d}_j, q) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_j \cap \mathcal{I}_q} \left[ \log \frac{\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q)}{1-\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q)} + \log \frac{1-\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q)}{\mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q)} \right] \]


We use pseudo-feedback: we take the top \(r\) returned documents as a training set \(S\).

\(r_i\): number of documents in \(S\) containing term \(i\).
\(n_i\): total number of documents containing term \(i\).

Initially (without feedback), we can take: \[ \mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q) = \text{constant} \quad\text{and}\quad \mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q) = \frac{n_i}{N} \] We then iterate with: \[ \mathbb{P}(t_i \mid R, q) = \frac{r_i}{r}, \qquad \mathbb{P}(t_i \mid \neg R, q) = \frac{n_i - r_i}{N - r} \]




The BIR model was extended to give the BM25 (Okapi) formula, widely used.
The weight of a term \(i\) for a query \(q\) is: \[ w_i^{\text{RSJ}} = \log \frac{(r_i + 0.5)(N - R - n_i + r_i + 0.5)}{(n_i - r_i + 0.5)(R - r_i + 0.5)} \] where \(R\) is the number of known (or estimated) relevant documents.
The return value for a document \(j\) is then: \[ \mathrm{RSV}(\mathbf{d}_j, q) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_q} w_i^{\text{RSJ}} \cdot \frac{(k_1+1) tf_{ij}}{K + tf_{ij}} \cdot \frac{(k_3+1) tf_{iq}}{k_3 + tf_{iq}} \] with \[ K = k_1 \left( (1-b) + b \cdot \frac{dl_j}{avdl} \right) \]

\(dl_j\): length of document \(j\) (number of words),
\(avdl\): average document length,
\(k_1\), \(b\), \(k_3\): parameters (typically \(k_1=1.2\), \(b=0.75\), \(k_3=7\) or \(1000\)).

title: Information Retrieval: Information Embedding
text:
The TF-IDF embedding has weaknesses:

Synonymy: different terms (e.g., “car”, “automobile”) should have close representations.
Polysemy: the same term (e.g., “table”) can have multiple meanings; it should be broken down into multiple concepts.

We seek a basis of \(K\) concepts \(\{\mathbf{c}_k\}_{k=1}^K\), orthonormal (\(\langle \mathbf{c}_k, \mathbf{c}_l \rangle = \delta_{kl}\)), such that each term is a linear combination of these concepts: \[ \mathbf{t}_i = \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha_{ki} \mathbf{c}_k \]



The Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of a matrix \(\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}\) is written: \[ \mathbf{W} = \mathbf{U} \mathbf{\Sigma} \mathbf{V}^\top \] where \(\mathbf{U}\) and \(\mathbf{V}\) are orthogonal and \(\mathbf{\Sigma}\) is diagonal containing the singular values \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_{\min(M,N)}\).
Truncated SVD of rank \(K\) consists of keeping only the first \(K\) columns of \(\mathbf{U}\) and \(\mathbf{V}\) and the \(K\) largest singular values: \[ \mathbf{W}_K = \mathbf{U}_K \mathbf{\Sigma}_K \mathbf{V}_K^\top \]



We apply SVD to the term-document matrix \(\mathbf{W}\) (e.g., TF-IDF). We set: \[ \mathbf{W}_K = \mathbf{U}_K \mathbf{\Sigma}_K \mathbf{V}_K^\top \]
Then:

The columns of \(\mathbf{U}_K\) represent the \(K\) concepts (orthonormal vectors in the term space).
The rows of \(\mathbf{V}_K\) are the coordinates of the documents in this concept space.
The singular values indicate the importance of each concept.

We can project a document \(\mathbf{d}_j\) (TF-IDF vector) into the concept space by: \[ \tilde{\mathbf{d}}_j = \mathbf{\Sigma}_K^{-1} \mathbf{U}_K^\top \mathbf{d}_j \] Similarly for a query \(\mathbf{q}\): \[ \tilde{\mathbf{q}} = \mathbf{\Sigma}_K^{-1} \mathbf{U}_K^\top \mathbf{q} \]
Cosine similarity is then calculated in this reduced space: \[ \mathrm{RSV}(\mathbf{d}_j, \mathbf{q}) = \frac{\langle \tilde{\mathbf{d}}_j, \tilde{\mathbf{q}} \rangle}{\|\tilde{\mathbf{d}}_j\| \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}\|} \]



The concept space depends on the initial collection. To add new documents, two strategies exist:



Let \(\mathbf{D}\) be the TF-IDF representation of the new documents.
Project \(\mathbf{D}\) onto the existing space: \(\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{U}_K^\top \mathbf{D}\).
Calculate the residual \(\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{U}_K \mathbf{P}\).
Find an orthonormal basis \(\mathbf{B}\) for \(\mathbf{H}\) (via QR, SVD).
Project \(\mathbf{H}\) onto this basis: \(\mathbf{J} = \mathbf{B}^\top \mathbf{H}\).
Form \(\mathbf{Q} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{\Sigma}_K & \mathbf{P} \\ \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{J} \end{bmatrix}\) and compute its SVD: \(\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{U}_n \mathbf{\Sigma}_n \mathbf{V}_n^\top\).
The new SVD is obtained by: \[ [\,\mathbf{U}_K \ \mathbf{B}\,] \mathbf{U}_n \mathbf{\Sigma}_n \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{V}_K^\top & \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{I} \end{bmatrix} = [\,\mathbf{W}_K \ \mathbf{D}\,] \]





Simply project the new documents onto the existing space: \[ \hat{\mathbf{D}} = \mathbf{U}_K^\top \mathbf{D} \]
Concatenate the old and new projections: \[ [\,\mathbf{\Sigma}_K \mathbf{V}_K^\top \ \ \hat{\mathbf{D}}\,] \approx \mathbf{U}_K^\top [\,\mathbf{W}_K \ \mathbf{D}\,] \] This approximation is less expensive but less accurate.

title: Information Retrieval: Information Embedding
text:
Relevance to a query is central in information retrieval.
Documents are embedded into a feature space via embeddings.
The Boolean (binary) model lacks flexibility.
The Bag of Words (BoW) model relies on frequencies.
Cosine distance extends set intersection.
Probabilistic models estimate term relevance.
Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI) decorrelates TF-IDF dimensions by discovering latent factors (concepts) via SVD.
Non-linear equivalents exist, based on neural networks.

title: Information Retrieval: Information Embedding
text:
What is the Retrieval Status Value (RSV)?
Why is the Boolean model not flexible?
Define term frequency and inverse document frequency.
What is the link between these quantities and a tag cloud?
What information do these factors provide?
Describe the structure of a probabilistic retrieval model.
How can logistic regression be used in information retrieval?
Why is the Binary Independence Retrieval (BIR) model so named?
What is the odds ratio?
What is a concept in the LSI model?
In what sense does LSI decorrelate features?
Explain the fold-in strategy.

title: Information Retrieval: Information Embedding
text: Information retrieval models are based on the notion of a term within a document. This applies to all types of media (text, image, audio…). The common objective is to estimate relevance. BoW, probabilistic, and LSI embeddings are constructed; neural embeddings are learned. All these models are classically implemented in software like Lucene.

title: Information Retrieval: Introduction
text:
The quantity of data produced each year reaches phenomenal orders of magnitude. We are talking about zettabytes, where
\[ 1 \text{ zettabyte} = 2^{70} \text{ bytes} = 10^{21} \text{ bytes} \approx 1 \text{ billion terabytes}. \]
This digital explosion concerns all domains: photos, videos, messages, transactions, etc.



The volume of photos taken each year illustrates this exponential growth. Millions, then billions of shots are captured daily, feeding massive databases.



Between 2012 and 2024, platforms like YouTube saw their uploaded content volume multiplied by 15 (going from 30 hours to 500 hours per minute). This trend underscores the crying need for effective methods to organize, search, and exploit these masses of information.






Informed decision-making relies on informed choices.
The information avalanche imposes advanced information management processes.
Access to large information reservoirs enables the emergence of Data Science.

It is therefore necessary to bring structure to raw data via:

An appropriate representation of documents.
Adequate similarity measures.
Analysis processes: mining, learning, visualization.





The notion of distance (or similarity) is fundamental for comparing documents or objects.
graph LR
    A[Document] --> B[Feature Extraction]
    B --> C[Feature Vector]
    D[Query] --> E[Feature Extraction]
    E --> F[Feature Vector]
    C --> G[Distance Calculation]
    F --> G
    G --> H[Results: closest documents]



Data Mining: unsupervised analysis (clustering, anomaly detection, imputation…).
Learning: supervised models (classification, regression…).
Visualization: dimensionality reduction to project data into an understandable space.

Features allow summarizing a document; distance allows comparing two documents (similarity, patterns) and also characterizing a document model (visualization).





The main objective of Information Retrieval (IR) is to respond to an information need expressed by a query. The goal is to automatically bring forth relevant information from a large collection of documents using a query formalism that is often flexible and not very constrained.





1950: Calvin N. Moors invents the term “Information Retrieval”.
1959: Hans Peter Luhn describes statistical retrieval (automatic indexing based on word frequencies).
1960: Maron and Kuhns define a probabilistic IR model.
1966: The Cranfield project establishes evaluation measures (recall, precision).
1968: Gerard Salton publishes the first book on the SMART system.
1972: Lockheed introduces DIALOG, a commercial online service.
Late 1980s: First PC systems integrating search capabilities.
Early 1990s: Cheap disks → storage revolution.
1992: Westlaw uses a large-scale probabilistic model.
Mid-1990s: Multimedia databases.
1994: Explosion of the Internet and the Web.
1995: IR techniques become ubiquitous (search button).
Today: Use of embeddings from machine learning for search.






Understand the basic models of information retrieval.
Understand social recommendation.
Master quality measures (evaluation).
Know the specificities of different media.
Overview of indexing techniques.
Overview of data visualization.

This course is part of the continuity of teachings in Data Science and Machine Learning.
